content.title: Playing badminton isn’t haram, so why could it still be a sin?
content.subtitle: Unknowingly inviting an unseen burden amidst the pure joy of winter nights.
content.body:
As winter evenings arrive, bright floodlights illuminate neighbourhood streets, open fields, and rooftops. The cold breeze, misty air, sound of rackets, flying shuttlecocks, and lively chatter of friends create a festive atmosphere. After a busy day, who doesn't enjoy playing badminton with friends or neighbours?

The Permissible Side of Exercise and Recreation

Islam is never against healthy recreation or physical exercise. Badminton is permissible when played for fitness and enjoyment, provided basic Islamic guidelines are followed: men must cover their bodies from the navel to the knees, there must be no gambling or betting, and obligatory prayers must not be neglected. It is a great way to stay active and refresh both body and mind.

The Hidden Shadows Beneath the Lights

The real concern begins when floodlights are installed to illuminate the courts. In many neighbourhoods, people illegally draw wires from main electricity lines on public roads or government poles to power high-voltage lights. This practice has become so common that few people question it. Besides being unlawful, such dangerous connections can also cause serious accidents.

The Rights of Millions and the Strict Ruling of Shariah

Thousands of units of electricity are wasted every day through these unauthorised connections. Electricity is a resource belonging to the entire nation. According to Islamic jurisprudence, using government electricity without proper authorisation and payment is ‘Ghasb’ (unlawful seizure) and theft, both completely haram.

Allah Almighty says: “Do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly.” (Surah Al-Baqarah: 188)

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) warned: “There are people who unlawfully spend the wealth granted by Allah (public funds); for them is Hell on the Day of Resurrection.” (Sahih al-Bukhari: 3118)

Taking someone's property may be forgiven by its owner. But unlawfully using public resources means violating the rights of millions. On the Day of Judgment, we cannot seek forgiveness from all of them. We will have to repay this debt with our good deeds. If those deeds run out, their sins will be placed upon us. (Sahih Muslim: 2581)

Common Excuses vs. The Reality of Shariah

To justify our actions, we often say: “The government commits injustice too. What's wrong with using a little electricity?” Or, “Our taxes pay for electricity anyway. Why shouldn't we use it?”

Think carefully. Does someone else's wrongdoing give us permission to do wrong? We will enter our graves alone, and no one will carry our burden of sin. Allah reminds us: “No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.” (Surah Al-An'am: 164)

Those who commit injustice will answer for every penny on the Day of Judgment. But using their actions as an excuse to violate others' rights makes us accountable too. Paying taxes does not mean we can use every public service for free. We pay electricity bills at home and at work, so why should a playground be any different?

Let the Joy Be Halal and Our Responsibility Be That of a Believer

May these misty winter nights bring us peace and happiness, not the burden of an unseen debt. May the lights illuminating our playgrounds never bring darkness to our records of deeds.

Let us connect electricity through our own household meters or pay the proper bill when taking a connection from a shop or home. A true believer is responsible not only on the prayer mat but also as a good citizen in every aspect of life. May Allah guide us to follow what is halal. Ameen.
